item.title: “Monks, how is it that Māra and his followers cannot reach? Here, monks, a monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states,…
item.description:
“Monks, how is it that Māra and his followers cannot reach? Here, monks, a monk, secluding himself from sensual desires, secluding himself from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, accompanied by initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of seclusion. This, monks, is called a monk who has blinded Māra, obliterated Māra’s track, leaving no trace, making Māra unable to find his path. Furthermore, monks, a monk, with the stilling of initial and sustained thought, enters and dwells in the second jhāna, which has internal confidence and unification of mind, without initial and sustained thought, with rapture and pleasure born of concentration. This is called a monk who has blinded Māra, obliterated Māra’s track, leaving no trace, making Māra unable to find his path.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 25 – Nivāpasutta

item.title: “Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove to a person who had just died. Monks, when he saw the corpse of a dead person, Prince…
item.description:
“Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove to a person who had just died. Monks, when he saw the corpse of a dead person, Prince Vipassī asked: ‘Good man, why is this person called dead?’ ‘Your Highness, he is called dead because now his mother, father, and other blood relatives no longer see him; and he no longer sees his mother, father, or other blood relatives.’ ‘Good man, then am I not dead — will I be subject to death? Will my father, mother, or other blood relatives not see me? And will I not see my father, mother, or other blood relatives?’ ‘Your Highness, you and I as well — even though we are not yet dead, we will die. Your father, mother, and other blood relatives will not see you, and you will not see your father, mother, or other blood relatives.’ ‘Good man, then this visit to the pleasure garden is enough. Drive back to the palace.’ ‘Yes, Your Highness.’ Monks, the charioteer, obeying the prince, drove back to the palace. Monks, Prince Vipassī returned to the palace, suffering, grieving, and thought: ‘Shameful indeed is this birth! And anyone who is born must age, must be sick, must die like this!’”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 14 – Mahāpadānasutta

item.title: The hunter set his trap and snare, The wise deer does not approach, Having eaten the crops, we go our way, Leaving the trapper to…
item.description:
The hunter set his trap and snare,
The wise deer does not approach,
Having eaten the crops, we go our way,
Leaving the trapper to lament.

From: Majjhima Nikāya 82 – Raṭṭhapālasutta

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that so gives rise to unarisen sensual desire, or to the increase and expansion of arisen sensual…
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, that so gives rise to unarisen sensual desire, or to the increase and expansion of arisen sensual desire, as the sign of the beautiful. The sign of the beautiful, monks, when unwisely attended to, gives rise to unarisen sensual desire and increases and expands arisen sensual desire.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.11
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: "Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the…
item.description:
"Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise — that cause the monk restrains, guards the mind faculty, practices the restraint of the mind faculty. By means of this noble restraint of the faculties, he experiences an internal feeling of ease, unblemished."

From: Dīgha Nikāya 2 – Sāmaññaphalasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what are the further things that should be done? ‘We must guard the sense faculties. When the eye sees a form, do not grasp…
item.description:
“Monks, what are the further things that should be done? ‘We must guard the sense faculties. When the eye sees a form, do not grasp the general feature, do not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the eye faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise—we will restrain that cause, guard the eye, practice restraint of the eye. When the ear hears a sound … nose smells an odor … tongue tastes a flavor … body feels a touch … mind cognizes phenomena, do not grasp the general feature, do not grasp the particular feature. Those causes whereby, if the mind faculty were not restrained, covetousness, sorrow, evil, unwholesome states would arise—we will restrain that cause, guard the mind, practice restraint of the mind.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 39 – Mahāhatthipadopamasutta
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects: ‘Whatever sensual pleasures present and future, whatever perceptions of sensual pleasure present and future, whatever forms present and future…
item.description:
“Furthermore, monks, a noble disciple reflects: ‘Whatever sensual pleasures present and future, whatever perceptions of sensual pleasure present and future, whatever forms present and future — all are the four great elements and form derived from the four great elements.’ While he practices thus, dwells often thus, his mind becomes serene in that element. With serene mind, he attains the Imperturbable (āneñja) either in this very life or he becomes strongly inclined to wisdom. At the breakup of the body, after death, it is possible that his consciousness, proceeding accordingly, may attain the Imperturbable.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 106 – Āneñjasappāyasutta

item.title: Form is like a lump of foam, Feeling like a water bubble, Perception like a mirage, Formations like a banana tree, Consciousness like a magic…
item.description:
Form is like a lump of foam,
Feeling like a water bubble,
Perception like a mirage,
Formations like a banana tree,
Consciousness like a magic trick —
So taught the Kinsman of the Sun.

If one reflects appropriately,
And rightly examines,
Seeing things as they really are,
Emptiness is clearly seen.

Beginning with this body,
As taught by the Great Sage,
When three things are abandoned,
Form is seen as discarded.

This body is discarded, unaware,
Not feeling, just heat and consciousness —
When thrown away, it lies,
Food for others.

This continuous body,
A magic trick, said the fool,
Is called a murderer —
No core can be found.

Thus should a monk contemplate the aggregates,
Ardent,
Both by day and by night,
Mindful and clearly comprehending.

He should abandon all fetters,
Make a refuge for himself,
Live as if his head were on fire,
Aspiring to the imperturbable state.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.95
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “And, monks, when that monk dwells in these five things, four more things should be developed. The perception of foulness should be developed to abandon…
item.description:
“And, monks, when that monk dwells in these five things, four more things should be developed. The perception of foulness should be developed to abandon greed; loving-kindness should be developed to abandon ill-will; mindfulness of breathing should be developed to cut off thoughts; the perception of impermanence should be developed to uproot the conceit ‘I am.’ For a monk with the perception of impermanence, monks, the perception of not-self becomes established. For one with the perception of not-self, the conceit ‘I am’ is uprooted, and Nibbāna is attained in this very life.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 9.1
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Elder Samiddhatta: “The five aggregates are fully understood, Their root is cut off. The wandering of birth is ended, Now there is no further becoming.”
item.description:
Elder Samiddhatta:
“The five aggregates are fully understood,
Their root is cut off.
The wandering of birth is ended,
Now there is no further becoming.”

From: Theragāthā 1.90
